steps.label: Instruction Sets
steps.content:
3.1 Computer Architecture

Instruction Sets

Year 10

  • Today: the commands a CPU can carry out, how they are stored in memory, and why a program made for one CPU may not run on another.
  • One small memory all lesson: address 6 holds 12, address 7 holds 30.
  • How this lesson works: on each slide, read the facts, predict, then read or watch why.
Think → Pair → ShareA game made for a games console will not run on a laptop, even when the files are copied across. Why might that be?Show the answer

Collect ideas: the two computers are built differently inside. Today shows one big reason, inside the CPU.

steps.label: Why a CPU Has a Fixed List
steps.content:
Why a CPU Has a Fixed List

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • The CPU from the last lessons can carry out only five commands: LOAD, ADD, SUB, STORE and OUTPUT.
  • Its CU and ALU have circuits for these commands, and no others.

items.prompt: Predict: a program asks this CPU to MULTIPLY. What happens?
options: It cannot process it: it is not one of its commands
The CU builds a new circuit for it
The ALU works out what MULTIPLY means
items.explain: A CPU can only process the commands it was built for. The list of all the commands a CPU can process is its instruction set. A multiplication must be made from commands it does have, such as ADD again and again.

steps.label: Exam Question: What Is an Instruction Set?
steps.content:
Exam Question: What Is an Instruction Set?

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2024, Question 5(b). Instructions are processed by a central processing unit (CPU) in a computer. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (b) The CPU uses an instruction set to decode the instruction. State what is meant by an instruction set.
scheme: A list of (machine code) commands that can be processed by the CPU
items.guidance: One mark. It must be a list of commands (or instructions) and say they can be processed (carried out, run) by the CPU. "The instructions in a program" earns no mark.
items.modelAnswer: A list of the commands that can be processed by the CPU.

steps.label: Why Instructions Are Binary
steps.content:
Why Instructions Are Binary

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • A program is stored in memory, just like data.
  • Memory can only store 0s and 1s.

items.prompt: Predict: how can the instruction LOAD 6 be stored in memory?
options: As a binary code for LOAD, then 6 in binary
As the word LOAD, written on the chip
It is not stored: the CU remembers it
items.explain: The instruction set gives each command its own binary code. An instruction written in this binary is machine code. Watch it happen on the next slide.

steps.label: Watch: LOAD 6 as Machine Code
steps.content:
Watch: LOAD 6 as Machine Code

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you watch: why can memory not just store the word LOAD?Show the answer

Memory is made of tiny switches that are on or off, 1 or 0. Everything stored has to be 0s and 1s.

Press Play, or Next for one step at a time.

steps.label: Explain It: Machine Code
steps.content:
Explain It: Machine Code

What to do: explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked, improve it, then press Submit answer.

items.context: The animation showed the instruction LOAD 6. Memory can only store 0s and 1s. The instruction set gives LOAD the binary code 0001, and 6 becomes 0110, so LOAD 6 is stored as 0001 0110. An instruction in binary is machine code. The first part (opcode) says which command; the second part (operand) says what to use. In your own words, explain what machine code is, and why a program is stored in memory as machine code.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain what machine code is, and why a program is stored in memory as machine code.
scheme: Machine code is instructions in binary // 0s and 1s
Memory or the CPU can only store or process binary // 0s and 1s
Each command in the instruction set has its own binary code
items.guidance: Any two points, one mark each. Credit each point in the student's own words; no technical words are needed. "It is a code" alone earns nothing: it must say binary, or 0s and 1s.
items.modelAnswer: Machine code is instructions in binary. Memory can only store 0s and 1s.

steps.label: Two Parts: Opcode and Operand
steps.content:
Two Parts: Opcode and Operand

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Each instruction is 8 bits.
  • This CPU's instruction set gives LOAD the code 0001 and ADD the code 0010.
0010 0111

items.prompt: Predict: what does 0010 0111 tell the CPU to do?
options: ADD the value at address 7
LOAD the value at address 2
ADD 2 and 7 together
items.explain: The first 4 bits, 0010, say which command: they are the opcode (ADD). The last 4 bits, 0111, say what to use: they are the operand, here the address 7 (4 + 2 + 1).

steps.label: Watch: Decoding 0010 0111
steps.content:
Watch: Decoding 0010 0111

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you watch: the CU has only 0s and 1s. How could it work out what to do?Show the answer

Ideas: split it into parts, look the parts up, turn binary into a number. Watch to check.

Press Play, or Next for one step at a time.

steps.label: Explain It: Decoding
steps.content:
Explain It: Decoding

What to do: explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked, improve it, then press Submit answer.

items.context: The animation showed 0010 0111 in the CIR. The CU split it into the opcode 0010 and the operand 0111. It looked up 0010 in the instruction set: ADD. The operand 0111 is address 7. Then the ALU added the value at address 7 (30) to the ACC (12), giving 42. In your own words, explain how the CU uses the instruction set to decode the instruction 0010 0111.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain how the CU uses the instruction set to decode the instruction 0010 0111.
scheme: The instruction is split into an opcode and an operand // 0010 and 0111
The CU looks up the opcode (0010) in the instruction set
It finds the command: 0010 means ADD
The operand 0111 gives what to use: the address 7
items.guidance: Any three points, one mark each. Credit each point in the student's own words. Point 3 needs the command (ADD) or that the opcode tells it which command; point 4 needs the operand to give the address or data.
items.modelAnswer: It is split into the opcode 0010 and the operand 0111. The CU looks up 0010 in the instruction set: ADD. The operand gives address 7.

steps.label: Check: Decode It
steps.content:
Check: Decode It

What to do: use the instruction set on the left. Split each instruction into opcode and operand.

The instruction set
OpcodeCommand
0001LOAD
0010ADD
0011SUB
0100STORE
0101OUTPUT

options: LOAD 9
LOAD 1
ADD 9
items.explain: Opcode 0001 is LOAD. Operand 1001 is 8 + 1 = 9. So LOAD 9: copy the value at address 9 into the ACC.

items.prompt: In 0011 0101, which part says which command to carry out?
options: 0101, the operand
0011, the opcode
Both parts together
items.explain: The opcode, 0011: SUB. The operand, 0101, gives the address 5.

steps.label: Exam Question: The Decode Stage
steps.content:
Exam Question: The Decode Stage

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2024, Question 5(b). A central processing unit (CPU) performs the fetch-decode-execute (FDE) cycle. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (b) Describe what happens at the decode stage of the cycle.
scheme: The CIR or CU receives the instruction from the MDR // the instruction is sent from the MDR to the CIR or CU
The instruction is separated into opcode and operand
The control unit decodes the instruction
items.guidance: Any three from the points, one mark each. A point marked ... follows on from the point before it.
items.modelAnswer: The instruction is separated into opcode and operand. The CU decodes it using an instruction set.

steps.label: Compare: Two CPU Types
steps.content:
Compare: Two CPU Types

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • A program is made for CPU A. Its first instruction is 0001 0110.
CPU A
OpcodeCommand
0001LOAD
0010ADD
0011SUB
0100STORE
0101OUTPUT
CPU B
OpcodeCommand
0001OUTPUT
0010LOAD
0011ADD
0100STORE

items.prompt: Predict: what does CPU B do with 0001 0110?
options: LOAD 6, the same as CPU A
OUTPUT: not what the program meant
It changes its list to match CPU A
items.explain: CPU B decodes with its own instruction set, where 0001 means OUTPUT. The same machine code means a different command on a CPU with a different instruction set, so the program does not do its job.

steps.label: Watch: One Program, Two CPUs
steps.content:
Watch: One Program, Two CPUs

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you watch: what else could go wrong when CPU B runs all three instructions?Show the answer

Make a guess for each instruction, then watch.

Press Play, or Next for one step at a time.

steps.label: Explain It: Two CPU Types
steps.content:
Explain It: Two CPU Types

What to do: explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked, improve it, then press Submit answer.

items.context: The animation ran the machine code 0001 0110, 0010 0111, 0101 0000 (made for CPU A) on CPU A and on CPU B. CPU A decoded LOAD 6, ADD 7, OUTPUT and output 42. CPU B has a different instruction set: for it 0001 is OUTPUT (it output 0), 0010 is LOAD (it loaded 30), and 0101 is not in its instruction set, so it could not process it. In your own words, explain why a machine code program made for CPU A may not run correctly on CPU B.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a machine code program made for CPU A may not run correctly on CPU B.
scheme: CPU B has a different instruction set
The same opcode or binary means a different command on CPU B
Some opcodes are not in CPU B's instruction set, so it cannot process them
The program must be made again for CPU B's instruction set
items.guidance: Any two points, one mark each. Credit each point in the student's own words. "CPU B is different" or "CPU B is slower" earns nothing: it must be about the instruction set, the commands or the codes.
items.modelAnswer: CPU B has a different instruction set, so the same opcode means a different command.

steps.label: Check: Which CPU Can Run It?
steps.content:
Check: Which CPU Can Run It?

What to do: pick an answer for each question. Ask: which instruction set was the machine code made for? Done when both are answered.

items.prompt: A machine code program was made for a CPU with instruction set X. Which CPU can run it correctly?
options: Any CPU with a faster clock
Any CPU with instruction set X
Any CPU with more cores
items.explain: Only a CPU with the same instruction set decodes every opcode to the same command. A faster clock or more cores does not change what the opcodes mean.

items.prompt: A program made for CPU A uses the opcode 0101. CPU B's instruction set has no 0101. What happens on CPU B?
options: CPU B cannot process that instruction
CPU B runs it as OUTPUT
CPU B adds 0101 to its list
items.explain: CPU B can only process commands in its own instruction set, so it cannot process 0101.
